Chapter 1 · A Letter to God

Chapter 1 of 33. G. L. Fuentes. A farmer, a hailstorm, a letter — and one of the sharpest ironies in the syllabus.

Open this chapter’s questions + MCQs →

🎯 Marks lens 📖 Deep concepts 🧠 Tricks ⚠️ Mistakes ❓ Exam Q&A ✍️ Task

🎯 Marks lens

Reference-to-context extracts and one 5-mark value-based long answer. The irony is always the question.
Know the numbers cold: Lencho asked for one hundred pesos, received seventy, and accused the post office employees of being 'a bunch of crooks'.

📖 Deep concepts

1. Summary. Lencho, a simple hardworking farmer, lives on the crest of a low hill in a Latin American valley, with his cornfield ripening and dotted with flowers. Rain comes — but it turns into a hailstorm that destroys the crop completely. Lencho's only hope is God, so he writes a letter asking for one hundred pesos to sow his field again and to live until the next harvest. The postmaster, a fat, amiable fellow, is moved by the farmer's faith, collects seventy pesos from his employees and friends, and sends the money in a letter signed 'God'. Lencho, on receiving the letter, is not surprised, but is angry at the shortfall: he writes a second letter asking God to send the rest directly, because the post office employees are a bunch of crooks.
2. Characters. Lencho — a simple, hardworking, unquestioning man of faith; his faith is absolute but so is his innocence. The postmaster — kind, generous and witty; he does not want to shake the farmer's faith in God. The employees and friends of the post office — they contribute out of charity, and are unjustly called crooks.
3. Themes. Unshakable faith — Lencho never doubts that God will answer. Irony — the very people who helped him are the ones he calls crooks. Human kindness and generosity — the postmaster's act is not duty but compassion. The gap between faith and reality.

🧠 Memory tricks

  • The word 'crooks' in the last line is the exam favourite. It means dishonest people — and the irony is that Lencho says it about the men who gave him money.
  • Two ironies, not one: the hailstorm destroys the crop that the rain was supposed to save; and the helpers are accused of theft.
  • Lencho is not grateful in the second letter — that surprise is worth a mark.

⚠️ Mistakes that cost marks

  • Saying Lencho received one hundred pesos. He received seventy.
  • Describing the postmaster as Lencho's relative or a government official on duty. He acted out of personal kindness.
  • Missing the word 'amiable' when describing the postmaster — examiners look for textual detail.

❓ Exam Q&A

3 marks Why did Lencho say the post office employees were a bunch of crooks?

Because he had asked God for one hundred pesos and received only seventy. His faith was so absolute that he could not believe God had made a mistake or had sent less, so he concluded that the post office employees must have taken the remaining thirty pesos. The irony is that these were the very men who had collected the money for him out of charity.

3 marks What made the postmaster decide to help Lencho?

He was moved by the farmer's unshakable faith in God. He did not want to shake that faith, so he collected money from his employees and friends, gave part of his own salary, and sent it to Lencho in a letter signed 'God'.

5 marks 'The story is built around two ironies.' Explain with reference to the text.

The first irony is in the weather: Lencho's field needed rain, and rain did come — but it turned into a hailstorm that destroyed the entire crop. The very thing that promised a good harvest took it away.
The second irony is in the ending: the post office employees, moved by Lencho's faith, collected seventy pesos and sent them to him. Lencho, finding the amount short, wrote back accusing those same men of stealing the money and calling them 'a bunch of crooks'. The helpers become the accused thieves, and the man who never doubted God doubts the honesty of human beings.

3 marks Was Lencho surprised to find a letter with money in it? What made him angry?

No, he was not surprised at all — he had expected an answer from God, and his confidence in God was so complete that receiving a reply seemed natural. What made him angry was that the envelope contained only seventy pesos instead of the hundred he had asked for. He was certain that God could not have made a mistake, so he concluded that the post office employees had taken the rest.

✍️ Hands-on task

Write the story in five sentences, then rewrite it from the postmaster's point of view in five sentences. The shift in perspective shows you who the real subject of the story is — and it is not Lencho.
